title: Al-Jahiz and the animals
hookLine: the witty writer of the Book of Animals

cards: Dog or rooster: which is the better creature? It sounds like an argument from the back of a school bus. In the Abbasid age, a writer from Basra put that argument into a huge book and let it run.
The dog's champion speaks. The rooster's champion answers. Each brings poems, proverbs, stories from hunters, and things he has watched with his own eyes.
Somewhere in the middle, the reader realizes this isn't really a book about winning. It's a book about looking. The writer was Amr ibn Bahr of Basra, and people knew him by a nickname: al-Jahiz.

teach.b: The nickname, tradition says, was about his eyes, which bulged.
He seems to have taken it with a grin, because wit runs through everything he wrote, including a whole book of stories about misers so tight-fisted they still get laughs.
But his great sprawling work is the Kitab al-Hayawan, the Book of Animals.
Open it anywhere and you find ants carrying grain, flies, mosquitoes, camels, dogs, birds, snakes.

Next to them, a line of poetry about the same creature, a verse of the Qur'an, a tale a sailor told, and then al-Jahiz telling you which parts he believes and which he doesn't. Why spend a life on gnats and roosters?
The Qur'an itself points at animals.
In Pickthall's translation: "There is not an animal in the earth, nor a flying creature flying on two wings, but they are peoples like unto you." Peoples: communities with their own ways.
Elsewhere it asks, "Will they not regard the camels, how they are created?" For a reader like al-Jahiz, looking closely at a creature was a way of reading signs of the One who made it.
So the smallest thing deserved a careful look, a second look, and a joke along the way.

teach.h: NOTHING TOO SMALL TO WONDER ABOUT.
teach.b: Nothing is too small or too strange to wonder about.
The ant counts. The mosquito counts. The dog lover and the rooster lover count, because both had to look hard to make their case.

how: The Qur'an speaks of animals among the signs of God, and al-Jahiz's Book of Animals is read today for its observation, its humor and its Arabic prose.

games.q: you're al-Jahiz. two men are arguing: the dog or the rooster, which is the better creature? you have a book to write. what do you do?
o: pick the dog and say why.
pick the rooster and say why.
let both champions make their full case.
games.why: he lets both sides speak at length, each with poems, stories and things seen with their own eyes. the debate is an excuse to look closely at both animals.

practice: If there's a creature near you, a pet, a bird at the window, a fly on the glass, watch it; if not, bring to mind one you've seen this week.
Notice how it moves, what it seems to want, what it does when it's still, without naming or judging, as if it were a whole people with its own ways.
If you pray, you can let the looking be a kind of thanks; if not, let it be plain attention.
